Chapter One: Childhood in a Divided World—Family, Fear, and First Questions.
You know, childhood usually brings to mind curiosity and discovery. But for some, it’s also filled with confusion—and a quiet sense of dread.
Picture a young boy, growing up in the Deep South during the early twentieth century. He can’t see the lines that divide his world, but he feels them all the same. Every breath feels heavy with rules that make no sense. Every day, he faces new puzzles: What’s safe? What’s forbidden? And who gets to decide, anyway?
In his small, crowded house, this restless child watches the adults shuffle through their daily routines. Worry and exhaustion hang over them. Hunger is always there, gnawing at the edges of every single day. Sometimes, the adults argue in quiet voices—about money, about work, about what’s fair and what isn’t. The boy senses that something is always just out of reach: a sense of safety, a full meal, maybe even a moment of peace.
One afternoon, his curiosity gets the better of him. He actually plays with fire—literally—and the fallout is fast and harsh. The grown-ups’ reaction goes beyond the danger itself. Their fear is deeper: in their world, even tiny mistakes can bring big trouble. The punishment is severe, and the lesson is clear. He learns to move with caution, to watch and listen before making any move.
Family life? It’s complicated. His mother is fiercely determined, but she’s tired—always struggling to keep the family together after his father walks away. That absence? It’s a wound that never really heals. His grandmother, deeply religious, tries to offer comfort through faith, but her strictness can feel like another set of chains. The house has rules—rigid ones. And questioning them? Not allowed. Still, the boy can’t help but wonder: Why are things the way they are?
School is a strange mix of refuge and battleground. He’s hungry to learn, but the classroom only highlights how different everyone is. Some teachers are gentle; others, quick to punish. The other kids, shaped by what’s happening outside, can be friendly one day and cruel the next. He learns to read the room, to navigate shifting friendships, always aware that one wrong move could make him a target.
Out in the world, things are even more dangerous. The streets are filled with people who look like him, but also with those who hold all the power. The rules out here aren’t written down, but everyone knows them. Say the wrong thing, look someone in the eye for too long—trouble finds you fast. He sees how grown-ups shrink themselves, avoiding attention and swallowing anger. He doesn’t quite get it yet, but he feels the weight of something bigger than himself.
As the boy grows, he starts to notice the patterns. Some folks are always in charge. Others are always nervous, always on edge. At night, he hears stories whispered in the dark—stories about violence, about unfairness, about dreams that never get a chance. The fear isn’t just about physical danger. It’s about knowing, deep down, that some lives simply matter less than others.
And yet, through all of this, the boy keeps asking questions. Why is the world like this? Why do some people have so much, and others so little? Why are certain doors always closed? The answers come slowly—if at all. But those questions, they become his armor. They’re a way to hold on to hope, even when the world feels hopeless.
